paras: The threatened lynching of Tom Manns, Ed Morris and Charles Sanders took place at Maysville, Kentucky, on February 3, 1903, when several hundred men followed the three Black prisoners from the jail to the railroad depot as officers moved them to Covington. The three were accused of robbing and shooting John B. Farrow, an aged farmer near Mt. Gilead, and officers held the crowd back with pistols. No one was hurt, and Kentucky papers reported the removal as a lynching prevented.

On the night of Sunday, February 1, robbers entered the Farrow home at Mt. Gilead in Fleming County, demanded money, bound the couple and shot Farrow, according to a Maysville wire. Maysville police arrested Thomas Manns, Charles Sanford and a third man the next night, and the Daily Public Ledger reported that Sanford had blamed Manns for the first shot. Early reports named John Sanford and his son Charles among the prisoners, but John Sanford was released on February 3 and Ed Morris was jailed in his place.
Talk of a lynching began at once: the wire said 'Feeling against the negroes is intense and a lynching is probable', and a Stanford paper wrote that 'a triple lynching will follow' if Farrow died.

On February 3 Manns and Sanders were taken before the grand jury, which indicted all three for burglary and for shooting with intent to kill after Sanders confessed. According to the Courier-Journal's Maysville correspondent, men from Farrow's neighborhood had been watching the jail, and a mob was openly expected that night from Mt. Carmel, Mt. Gilead and Orangeburg. Officers instead moved the prisoners that afternoon, at 4:20 p.m. by the Ledger's account, 'to avoid any further trouble'.

The same correspondent wrote that 'several hundred excited men' followed the prisoners to the depot, that officers kept them back with pistols, and that the 'demonstrations' there 'made them tremble'. Charles G. Calvert, described as a prominent farmer of Orangeburg, was arrested for his 'frantic' efforts to stop the removal. The prisoners reached the Covington jail, where Sanders later gave a second confession blaming Mann and Morris.

No later report of a charge or hearing against Calvert was found. The three stayed in Covington until June, when the sheriff asked for state troops, fearing the prisoners 'would be lynched by enraged citizens'. A Frankfort dispatch reported that an armed mob had gathered at the Maysville station in early June when word spread that the men were to be brought back, and a Maysville wire put the crowd at their June 16 arrival at more than 5,000.

Tried under guard of troops, Sanders pleaded guilty and Manns and Morris were convicted, each receiving five years for shooting with intent to kill. Mann and Morris received ten more years each for burglary, Sanders' burglary charge was continued, and the troops took the prisoners to Frankfort. The Ledger congratulated Maysville and Mason County that 'the mob spirit has been suppressed', crediting Farrow's family with urging obedience to the law.

The fullest account of the depot crowd was a special in the Louisville Courier-Journal headed 'Lynching Prevented by Prompt Action of Maysville Officers', which also carried the deck 'Lynching at Maysville Prevented by Removal of Farrow Assailants to Covington' on its front page. That report described the mob's plans openly and identified the prisoners only as 'all colored'. The Maysville Daily Public Ledger, by contrast, said nothing of a crowd, recording only that the men were moved 'for safe keeping'.

Elsewhere the story ran as short items: a wire headed 'LYNCHING PROBABLE' in the Montgomery Advertiser before the transfer, and a one-line note in the Mt. Sterling Advocate that the men had been moved 'to prevent a lynching'. No Black-press report of the February crowd was found; the St. Louis Palladium and the State Ledger noticed the case only in June, when troops guarded the trial.
The crowd at the depot, the drawn pistols and Calvert's arrest appear only in the Courier-Journal special; the local Ledger neither confirms nor denies them.

reader.title: Threatened lynching of Tom Manns, Ed Morris and Charles Sanders (February 1903)
bases: A crowd gathered to take three Black prisoners from the Maysville jail and was held off while officers moved them to Covington 'to avoid a mob' (A5, A9); no one was killed, so this is a threatened lynching.

No one was killed: the three prisoners were moved to Covington before the expected mob came (A5, A6) and were tried in June (A15, A16). The episode is a threatened lynching by 'several hundred excited men' acting on the accusation of the Farrow shooting (A5).

The transfer to Covington is reported by the local Ledger (A6) and the Courier-Journal (A5), and A9 independently gives its purpose as 'to prevent a lynching'; the depot crowd, the pistols and Calvert's arrest rest on the Courier-Journal special alone (A5), and the Ledger mentions no crowd (A6).

accounts.label: Kentucky news briefs
accounts.gist: A lynching was forecast if Farrow died, and the removal was 'to prevent a lynching'.

framing.detail: The Courier-Journal credited 'Prompt Action of Maysville Officers' and reported the mob's plans openly while calling the accused 'all colored'.
The Maysville Ledger praised the police for the arrests and played down the crowd; in June it congratulated citizens that 'the mob spirit has been suppressed'.
Out-of-state papers ran a wire forecasting a lynching ('LYNCHING PROBABLE'), and state briefs said a 'triple lynching will follow' if Farrow died.
The only Black-press items found concern the June trial and troops, not the February crowd.
